shipped_row.boundary_rationale: The narrator's report that “After this Job opened his mouth, and cursed the day of his birth.” (web:Job.3.1) is followed at once by the dialogue-formula “Job answered:” (web:Job.3.2; Hebrew וַיַּ֥עַן אִיּ֗וֹב וַיֹּאמַֽר), a doubled introduction to the same speech-act: a mouth-opening idiom (פָּתַ֤ח אִיּוֹב֙ אֶת פִּ֔יהוּ) paired with the vaya'an-formula proper. Both verses stand apart in register from the wholly poetic curse that opens at 3:3, and together they mark the turn from the silence that closes 2:13 (“So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.” web:Job.2.13) to Job's own voice.
shipped_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Split the pair at the Masoretic paragraph break following 3:1 into two one-verse rows, Job.3.1-Job.3.1 and Job.3.2-Job.3.2, honoring that (single-witness) division over the shared introductory function argued here.
shipped_row.literature_type_guess: discourse frame: narrative mouth-opening and dialogue formula

prev_row.boundary_rationale: Job's three friends enter by name, אֱלִיפַ֤ז הַתֵּימָנִי֙ וּבִלְדַּ֣ד הַשּׁוּחִ֔י וְצוֹפַ֖ר הַנַּֽעֲמָתִ֑י (oshb:Job.2.11): Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite, “and they made an appointment together to come to sympathize with him and to comfort him” (web:Job.2.11). Their approach and grief are narrated at web:Job.2.12, “they raised their voices, and wept” before the row closes on the seven-day silent vigil, “So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great” (web:Job.2.13). This unit's closing edge rests on the wordlessness Job.2.13 states outright -- “no one spoke a word to him” -- which is broken precisely at the seam with web:Job.3.1, where the temporal marker אַחֲרֵי כֵ֗ן ('after this') reopens Job's own voice, ending the vigil's silence with his extended lament.
prev_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading through into Job's lament was considered, but the seven-day silence this row records is broken specifically by the temporal marker that reopens his voice after the vigil.
prev_row.literature_type_guess: three friends arrive: gathering and seven-day silence

next_row.boundary_rationale: The curse proper opens with the jussive incipit “Let the day perish in which I was born, the night which said, ‘There is a boy conceived.” (web:Job.3.3; Hebrew יֹ֣אבַד י֭וֹם, ‘let the day perish’), a form independently swept at 1 occurrence book-wide (sweep: 1 book-wide, byte tier), and runs a chain of day/night imprecations through “because it didn’t shut up the doors of my mother’s womb, nor did it hide trouble from my eyes.” (web:Job.3.10), which closes the chain by giving its motive (the day did not shut the womb). The next verse turns from cursing the day to interrogating Job's own birth, a distinct topic marked at its own opening (the seam at 3:10|3:11).
next_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Break the curse chain at 3:6|3:7 was weighed differently from 3:8|3:9: 3:7 does open with a verse-initial presentative, הִנֵּ֤ה הַלַּ֣יְלָה הַ֭הוּא יְהִ֣י גַלְמ֑וּד אַל תָּבֹ֖א רְנָנָ֣ה בֽוֹ (oshb:Job.3.7), a tier-1 signal class in its own right, but it governs the same subject 3:6 has already introduced -- both verses open on 'that night' (הַלַּ֥יְלָה הַהוּא֮ יִקָּחֵ֪ה֫וּ אֹ֥פֶל אַל יִ֭חַדְּ בִּימֵ֣י שָׁנָ֑ה בְּמִסְפַּ֥ר יְ֝רָחִ֗ים אַל יָבֹֽא, oshb:Job.3.6) -- so the presentative resumes the day/night imprecation rather than turning to a new topic, and the chain is kept whole through it. No interrogative, vocative, or formula marks 3:8|3:9.
next_row.literature_type_guess: curse strophe: day perish and night imprecation opening

trigger_evidence.sentence: WEB's trailing 'saying,' bridges the two verses in translation only.

shipped_row.boundary_rationale: The quoted voice's oracle opens “Shall mortal man be more just than God? Shall a man be more pure than his Maker?” (web:Job.4.17; Hebrew הַֽ֭אֱנוֹשׁ מֵאֱל֣וֹהַ יִצְדָּ֑ק, a byte-true interrogative-he construction -- the row's own near-edge driver, since 4:16's closing clause דְּמָמָ֖ה וָק֣וֹל אֶשְׁמָֽע (oshb:Job.4.16) carries no verb of speaking and belongs to no formula family; WEB's trailing 'saying,' bridges the two verses in translation only. The oracle runs to “Isn’t their tent cord plucked up within them? They die, and that without wisdom.” (web:Job.4.21), which closes the embedded speech. Eliphaz's own voice resumes with a fresh imperative topic-turn at 5:1 (qra na), the seam bounding this row's far edge.
shipped_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Carry the oracle through 5:1 as one continuous unit, since both open with rhetorical questions, but 5:1's qra na addresses Job directly in Eliphaz's own voice, not the vision's.
shipped_row.literature_type_guess: night-voice oracle: mortal frailty against divine judgment

prev_row.boundary_rationale: “Now a thing was secretly brought to me. My ear received a whisper of it.” (web:Job.4.12; Hebrew וְ֭אֵלַי דָּבָ֣ר יְגֻנָּ֑ב) turns to Eliphaz's own night-vision testimony, a personal-voice register distinct from the preceding proverb. The strophe narrates the experience of the vision through its close, “It stood still, but I couldn’t discern its appearance. A form was before my eyes. Silence, then I heard a voice, saying,” (web:Job.4.16), whose final clause (דְּמָמָ֖ה וָק֣וֹל אֶשְׁמָֽע, ‘silence, then a voice I heard’) is a discourse frame introducing direct speech -- a perception clause with no verb of speaking, not a member of the book's verse-initial vayomer formula family; the quoted content itself begins at 4:17, not before.
prev_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Fold 4:17-4:21 into this row on the ground that the vision is one continuous unit through 4:21, but the shift from narrated experience to quoted oracle is itself marked by the discourse frame closing 4:16b -- a perception clause, not a member of the book's verse-initial vayomer formula family -- and deserves its own row.
prev_row.literature_type_guess: night-vision narrative: Eliphaz's oracle frame strophe

next_row.boundary_rationale: “Call now; is there any who will answer you? To which of the holy ones will you turn?” (web:Job.5.1; Hebrew קְֽרָא נָ֭א, ‘call now’) opens an imperative challenge paralleling the zkhor na of 4:7 (both topic-turn imperatives addressed to Job), and the strophe illustrates the fool's perishing down to “but man is born to trouble, as the sparks fly upward.” (web:Job.5.7), a proverbial close on man's trouble-bound birth. The following verse turns to Eliphaz's own stance with an adversative-plus-pronoun opening, marking the far edge.
next_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Split the fool's-fate illustration of 5:2-5:7 from the opening challenge of 5:1 as its own row, but the challenge and its illustration share one interrogative frame with no internal topic-turn.
next_row.literature_type_guess: fool's-fate strophe: uncontained wrath leads to ruin

shipped_row.boundary_rationale: A third-person topic shift opens the row: “To him who is ready to faint, kindness should be shown from his friend; even to him who forsakes the fear of the Almighty.” web:Job.6.14 (Hebrew לַמָּ֣ס מֵרֵעֵ֣הוּ חָ֑סֶד וְיִרְאַ֖ת שַׁדַּ֣י יַעֲזֽוֹב, oshb:Job.6.14, grammatically third-person throughout -- the friend-word carries a 3ms suffix and the verb is 3ms imperfect, with no vocative particle), pivoting the subject-matter from Job's own exhaustion to a gnomic charge against companions in general. He extends the charge with the brook-caravan metaphor, “My brothers have dealt deceitfully as a brook, as the channel of brooks that pass away;” web:Job.6.15, traces the image through the melting ice and vanishing caravans of web:Job.6.16-Job.6.20, then the address itself turns second-person for the first time in the unit, “For now you are nothing. You see a terror, and are afraid.” web:Job.6.21 (Hebrew כִּֽי עַ֭תָּה הֱיִ֣יתֶם לא ל֑וֹ תִּֽרְא֥וּ חֲ֝תַ֗ת וַתִּירָֽאוּ, oshb:Job.6.21, all second-person plural), before closing on a pair of denials that he ever asked the friends for a gift or ransom, web:Job.6.22-Job.6.23. This second-person address shift at 6:21 is a genuine tier-1 signal, not mere texture; it runs unbroken to the end of the chapter, and it is disclosed here as a live internal candidate for this unit's own seam rather than dismissed. It is not adopted as the row's own edge because the third-person charge and its direct application are held together as one movement of the friend-rebuke closing on Job's self-examination through 6:23; the alternative seam at 6:20|6:21 is disclosed here as a live, comparably warranted rival rather than resolved.
shipped_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking the row at Job.6.20|Job.6.21 for the second-person turn there is a live rival, not a texture-only consideration: 6:21 opens the unit's first 2mp forms and second-person address runs unbroken through 6:29 (nine verses, Job.6.21-Job.6.29), a comparably or better-warranted internal seam than the 6:23|6:24 edge kept here. It is disclosed rather than adopted because the row is held as one continuous rebuke of the friends across the third-person charge and its direct application; the question is left open rather than resolved, in the same spirit as the frame's own disclosed 2:6|2:7 crux.
shipped_row.literature_type_guess: friends rebuke: why abandon one brought low and helpless

prev_row.boundary_rationale: A topic-turn interrogative-wish opens the row: מִֽי יִ֭תֵּן תָּב֣וֹא שֶֽׁאֱלָתִ֑י וְ֝תִקְוָתִ֗י יִתֵּ֥ן אֱלֽוֹהַּ (oshb:Job.6.8), an instance of the dialogue-wide mi-yitten wish formula (sweep: 9 verses book-wide, 10 tokens, one verse carrying two, independently re-swept at skeleton tier). Job spells the wish out as a plea to be let go and cut off web:Job.6.9, holds his one consolation to be that he has “not denied the words of the Holy One” web:Job.6.10, then turns to a run of rhetorical questions about his exhausted capacity, “What is my strength, that I should wait? What is my end, that I should be patient?” web:Job.6.11, “Is my strength the strength of stones? Or is my flesh of bronze?” web:Job.6.12, closing on the admission that “wisdom is driven away from me” web:Job.6.13. The row ends before the next strophe's turn from Job's own exhausted capacity to a third-person accusation of the friends, opening at Job.6.14.
prev_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the row through Job.6.14 would merge the wish-formula lament with the brook-metaphor rebuke of the friends that follows it.
prev_row.literature_type_guess: death wish strophe: Job seeks release from torment

next_row.boundary_rationale: An imperative shift opens the row: ה֭וֹרוּנִי וַאֲנִ֣י אַחֲרִ֑ישׁ וּמַה שָּׁ֝גִ֗יתִי הָבִ֥ינוּ לִֽי (oshb:Job.6.24), Job's invitation to be corrected rather than the denial he had just voiced. He weighs “words of uprightness” against the friends' empty reproof web:Job.6.25, protests that their reproof treats the speeches of one who is desperate as mere wind while they would gamble away the fatherless web:Job.6.26-Job.6.27, then appeals directly, “Now therefore be pleased to look at me, for surely I will not lie to your face.” web:Job.6.28, repeats the appeal, “Please return. Let there be no injustice. Yes, return again. My cause is righteous.” web:Job.6.29, and closes on a self-examining question, “Is there injustice on my tongue? Can’t my taste discern mischievous things?” web:Job.6.30. The row runs from the imperative petition to the end of the chapter, closing Job's rebuke of the friends before the reply turns, in the next chapter, to a meditation on human toil in general.
next_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying the row back to include the brook-metaphor rebuke above it would stretch one strophe well past a comfortable length without an intervening tier-1 seam to justify the span. A second rival was weighed at this row's own near edge: 6:28 opens with the ve'attah turn, וְ֭עַתָּה הוֹאִ֣ילוּ פְנוּ בִ֑י וְעַל פְּ֝נֵיכֶ֗ם אִם אֲכַזֵּֽב (oshb:Job.6.28) -- a device that sweeps 8 book-wide (Job.6.28, Job.30.1, Job.30.9, Job.30.16, Job.35.15, Job.37.21, Job.42.5, Job.42.8) and keys strophe structure elsewhere in the book -- followed at 6:29 by an imperative-plus-na, שֻֽׁבוּ נָ֭א אַל תְּהִ֣י עַוְלָ֑ה ושבי וְשׁ֥וּבוּ ע֝וֹד צִדְקִי בָֽהּ (oshb:Job.6.29), the same form-class opening 5:1 (קְֽרָא נָ֭א) and 4:7 (זְכָר נָ֗א). Splitting at 6:27|6:28 was rejected because 6:28's appeal ('look at me... I will not lie to your face') and 6:29's renewed imperative ('return... my cause is righteous') both continue rather than reopen the direct appeal Job begins at 6:24 -- one imperative-headed appeal running from ה֭וֹרוּנִי at 6:24 through the self-examining close at 6:30 -- so the row is kept whole through both internal signals rather than split at either.
next_row.literature_type_guess: Job appeals: teach me what error caused this punishment

shipped_row.boundary_rationale: A topic-turn interrogative opens the row's final movement: מָֽה אֱ֭נוֹשׁ כִּ֣י תְגַדְּלֶ֑נּוּ וְכִי תָשִׁ֖ית אֵלָ֣יו לִבֶּֽךָ (oshb:Job.7.17), “What is man, that you should magnify him, that you should set your mind on him,” web:Job.7.17, continuing the direct address to God with the daily scrutiny of web:Job.7.18, the plea “How long will you not look away from me” web:Job.7.19, and the accusation of being made a “mark” and a “burden” web:Job.7.20 -- a verse that itself carries a paseq segment, tier-3 and single-witness -- closing the speech on “Why do you not pardon my disobedience, and take away my iniquity? prev_row.boundary_rationale: An emphatic self-reference opens a new resolve: גַּם אֲנִי֮ לֹ֤א אֶחֱשָׂ֫ךְ פִּ֥י אֲֽ֭דַבְּרָה בְּצַ֣ר רוּחִ֑י אָ֝שִׂ֗יחָה בְּמַ֣ר נַפְשִֽׁי (oshb:Job.7.11), “Therefore I will not keep silent. I will speak in the anguish of my spirit. I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.” web:Job.7.11. Job asks “Am I a sea, or a sea monster, that you put a guard over me?” web:Job.7.12, describes a bed that fails to comfort him because God frightens him with dreams web:Job.7.13-Job.7.14, and concludes that his soul “chooses strangling, death rather than my bones” web:Job.7.15, then states outright, “I loathe my life. I don’t want to live forever. Leave me alone, for my days are but a breath.” web:Job.7.16. The row runs from the fronted-pronoun resolve to the loathing-of-life statement it produces, ending before the next topic-turn interrogative.
prev_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending the row at Job.7.10 would cut the fronted-pronoun resolve of Job.7.11 away from the dream-terror and life-loathing material it introduces.
prev_row.literature_type_guess: mortality complaint: days flee like fleeting wind patterns

next_row.boundary_rationale: The verse-initial formula וַ֭יַּעַן בִּלְדַּ֥ד הַשּׁוּחִ֗י וַיֹאמַֽר (oshb:Job.8.1) hands the speech to Bildad; the WEB rendering is “Then Bildad the Shuhite answered,” web:Job.8.1. Bildad's vaya'an-formula family sums to three speeches book-wide across two gentilic spellings, named per member: the plene הַשּׁוּחִ֗י opening this verse (byte tier; the plene spelling itself sweeps 3 book-wide at 2:11, 8:1, 42:9, but only 8:1 is a formula opening), and the defective הַשֻּׁחִ֗י opening his later two speeches, oshb:Job.18.1 and oshb:Job.25.1 (byte tier; sweeps 2 book-wide). The family total of three formula members is a sum across these two named spellings, not one blended string. Bildad rebukes Job's outburst, “How long will you speak these things? Shall the words of your mouth be a mighty wind?” web:Job.8.2, states his retribution doctrine as a rhetorical denial, “Does God pervert justice? Or does the Almighty pervert righteousness?” web:Job.8.3, applies it to Job's dead children web:Job.8.4, and offers the conditional promise that follows from the doctrine, “If you want to seek God diligently, make your supplication to the Almighty.” web:Job.8.5, “If you were pure and upright, surely now he would awaken for you, and make the habitation of your righteousness prosperous.” web:Job.8.6, closing on the promise that “your latter end would greatly increase” web:Job.8.7. The row runs from the speech formula through the doctrine's opening statement, ending before Bildad turns to an appeal to ancestral precedent.
next_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating Job.8.1 as its own row would separate Bildad's formula from the doctrine it introduces without a competing tier-1 signal before the imperative appeal to precedent that follows.
next_row.literature_type_guess: Bildad opens: ancient wisdom on retribution doctrine

next_row.boundary_rationale: A topic-turn interrogative opens the nature parable: הֲיִֽגְאֶה גֹּ֭מֶא בְּלֹ֣א בִצָּ֑ה יִשְׂגֶּה אָ֥חוּ בְלִי מָֽיִם (oshb:Job.8.11), “Can the papyrus grow up without mire? Can the rushes grow without water?” web:Job.8.11. Bildad extends the plant image through its premature withering web:Job.8.12, applies it to “all who forget God” whose hope is a “spider's web” web:Job.8.13-Job.8.14, describes a house that will not stand web:Job.8.15, and elaborates a second plant image of roots wrapped around a rock pile web:Job.8.16-Job.8.17, ending on the plant's erasure from its place and the ironic close, “Behold, this is the joy of his way. Out of the earth, others will spring.” web:Job.8.18-Job.8.19. The presentative הן also opens Job.8.20 immediately after (הֶן אֵ֭ל לֹ֣א יִמְאַס תָּ֑ם וְלֹֽא יַ֝חֲזִ֗יק בְּיַד מְרֵעִֽים, oshb:Job.8.20) -- but 8:20 is third person throughout, its two finite verbs both 3ms with no second-person morpheme. The shift this row's edge actually rests on is the grammatical subject, not the addressee: 8:11-8:19 traces the fate of 'him who forgets God' in the third person through a plant figure, and 8:20 closes that figure with a hen-headed maxim whose subject becomes God himself (still third person) -- a different pivot from the direct second-person promise that follows one verse later, at 8:21 (inside the next row). One further nuance on this row's own near edge: 8:18 itself closes on לֹ֣א רְאִיתִֽיךָ, a second-person suffix, but it sits inside the plant-figure's own quoted denial rather than the narrator's direct address to Job, so the third-person/second-person contrast this row's edges draw is not perfectly morphological on either side, and is disclosed as such.
next_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the row through Job.8.20-22 would run the third-person plant parable together with the hen-headed maxim's subject-shift to God at 8:20 and the direct second-person promise that follows it at 8:21, erasing a genuine grammatical turn even though that turn is a subject shift rather than an address shift at its own opening verse.
